title: Takeda's AI-Designed Psoriasis Pill Clears Skin 2.5 Times Better Than Rival — What It Means for South Asians
excerpt: The once-daily oral drug zasocitinib outperformed the market leader in a landmark head-to-head trial, offering hope for an underdiagnosed community
body:
Takeda Pharmaceutical has announced results from its head-to-head Phase 3 clinical trial that could reshape how psoriasis is treated worldwide — and the implications for South Asian patients are particularly significant.

The Japanese drugmaker's experimental oral pill, zasocitinib (also known as TAK-279), outperformed the current market-leading oral psoriasis treatment deucravacitinib (sold as Sotyktu by Bristol Myers Squibb) by a wide margin in the LATITUDE Atlas study. More than 35 percent of patients taking zasocitinib achieved complete skin clearance at 16 weeks — over 2.5 times the response rate of deucravacitinib. The drug also hit every key secondary endpoint, including near-complete clearance and physician-assessed remission scores.

## A Once-Daily Pill That Could Replace Injections

Until recently, patients with moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis had two choices: topical creams that often proved inadequate, or injectable biologics that are effective but expensive, inconvenient, and carry immune-suppression risks. Deucravacitinib, approved in 2022, was the first oral pill to offer a middle path, but its efficacy — roughly 15 percent complete clearance — left considerable room for improvement.

Zasocitinib belongs to the same drug class (TYK2 inhibitors) but was designed with the help of artificial intelligence to be more selective and potent. Takeda acquired the molecule from Nimbus Therapeutics in a deal worth up to $6 billion, signalling the company's conviction in the drug's potential. Analysts project peak annual sales of $3 billion to $6 billion.

"In this head-to-head study, zasocitinib clearly demonstrated superior skin clearance compared with deucravacitinib, highlighting clinically meaningful differences within the oral treatment class," said Dr Linda Stein Gold, Director of Dermatology Clinical Research at Henry Ford Health and principal investigator for the trial.

## Why This Matters for the South Asian Diaspora

Psoriasis affects an estimated 0.1 to 0.5 percent of South Asians — lower than Western populations on paper, but widely believed to be underdiagnosed due to how the condition presents on darker skin tones. Plaques on brown skin often appear purple or dark brown rather than the classic pink-red, leading to delayed diagnosis and treatment.

More critically, research from India shows that 44 percent of psoriasis patients in South India also have metabolic syndrome, a cluster of conditions including insulin resistance, obesity, and high blood pressure. Psoriasis and Type 2 diabetes share genetic risk factors, making the disease a compound health burden for a community already disproportionately affected by diabetes.

For NRIs in the United States, access to an effective oral treatment could be transformative. Injectable biologics like adalimumab or secukinumab can cost $50,000 to $80,000 per year before insurance, require cold-chain storage, and demand regular clinic visits. A once-daily pill that delivers superior clearance rates could dramatically reduce both the financial and logistical burden of managing psoriasis.

## Safety and the Road to Approval

In the LATITUDE Atlas trial, zasocitinib was "generally well tolerated" with no new safety signals, Takeda said. The safety profile was consistent with earlier Phase 3 studies in the company's broader development programme.

Takeda plans to submit a New Drug Application to the U.S. Food and Drug Administration and other regulatory agencies starting this fiscal year, with detailed data to be presented at upcoming dermatology conferences. If approved, zasocitinib would become the most effective oral treatment for plaque psoriasis ever brought to market.

## What's Next

The drug still faces the regulatory gauntlet, and pricing will ultimately determine real-world access. But for the roughly 7.5 million Americans living with psoriasis — including a significant and underserved South Asian population — the prospect of a pill that clears skin completely in more than one in three patients represents a genuine step change. For NRI families managing psoriasis alongside diabetes and cardiovascular risk, that could mean fewer injections, fewer side effects, and a simpler path to clearer skin.
